title: Play Through Children’s Eyes—The Subjective Meaning of Play to Young Children
text_snippet: Play Through Children’s Eyes—The Subjective Meaning of Play to Young Children Abstract Play is fundamental to children’s daily activities and provides a critical avenue for learning and development. However, attempts to describe and operationalize play are dominated by adults’ perspectives. This study aims to explore the subjective meaning of play to young children. Using a qualitative approach, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 327 children aged 4 to 8 years from [a Western European country]. These interviews were analyzed using both deductive and inductive content analysis methods to categorize children’s descriptions of play. Approximately half of the children provided coherent, differentiated descriptions of play. Results indicate that children’s perceptions align deductively with the features of play seminally defined by Krasnor and Pepler (1980) and expanded by Smith and Vollstedt (1985): positive affect, flexibility, intrinsic motivation, nonliterality, and means before end. The inductive analysis identified three additional categories, children’s business, social interactions, and object reference and therefore revealed additional features of play relevant for children. title: Sensor Technology to Measure Social Engagement for Children with Behavioral Challenges
text_snippet: Sensor Technology to Measure Social Engagement for Children with Behavioral Challenges Abstract Social engagement is crucial for preschool children’s social, cognitive, and language development. Children with behavioral challenges or children who are English Language Learners (ELL) may experience difficulty in making meaningful social connections in inclusive preschool classrooms. Teachers often face challenges in continuously observing each child’s social engagement in early childhood education settings. Therefore, this exploratory study examined the social engagement patterns of preschool children across structured and unstructured activity periods using the Wearable Human Interaction Tracker (WHIT) sensor system. The study was conducted in an inclusive preschool classroom and included one target child with behavioral challenges who was also an ELL and five of his peers without social challenges. We compared the social engagement patterns of the target child with those of his peers. Results showed that the target child exhibited distinct patterns of social connectivity, peer-specific interactions, initiation and termination behaviors, and classroom area preferences compared to those of his peers. title: Thinking Through Making: Supporting Children’s Inquiry Through Visual Arts in Early Childhood Education
text_snippet: Thinking Through Making: Supporting Children’s Inquiry Through Visual Arts in Early Childhood Education Abstract Inquiry-based approaches in early childhood education recognise the visual arts as a vital mode of thinking, enabling children to theorise, represent, and make meaning through material and sensory exploration. However, integrating the arts meaningfully within inquiry can be complex, and teachers may find this difficult to navigate. This article draws on findings from a multi-year collaborative research project conducted across six early childhood settings in Aotearoa New Zealand, examining how inquiry-based approaches were interpreted in practice. The study identifies the visual arts and material exploration as multimodal pathways for children’s theorising, reflection, and community connection, grounded in relationships with local people, places, and materials. Building on these insights, the article proposes a framework, Thinking Through Visual Inquiry , which conceptualises how the visual arts support inquiry as a relational, recursive, and evolving process. The framework includes two articulations, one for infants and toddlers, and one for young children, highlighting how artistic processes function as modes of thinking across phases of inquiry. title: School Readiness and Home Visiting: A Scoping Review of Definitions, Outcomes, and Contextual Moderators
text_snippet: School Readiness and Home Visiting: A Scoping Review of Definitions, Outcomes, and Contextual Moderators Abstract This scoping review examined empirical research on the relationship between participation in home visiting programs and children’s school readiness at the time of school entry. Specifically, we explored how school readiness is defined across studies, which domains are assessed as outcomes, and what contextual factors moderate the effects of home visiting on school readiness. School readiness is a multidimensional construct encompassing physical well-being, social-emotional development, language and literacy, approaches to learning, and cognitive skills. Home visiting programs aim to promote early development and family well-being, yet evidence remains mixed regarding their impact on school readiness and the contextual factors that shape these outcomes. This review addresses these gaps by mapping the scope and characteristics of existing research. A systematic search of CINAHL Plus, Embase, PubMed, and Scopus was conducted for articles published between January 2016 and April 2025. title: Building a Strong Math Foundation: Supporting Early Math Precursors for Babies and Toddlers
text_snippet: Building a Strong Math Foundation: Supporting Early Math Precursors for Babies and Toddlers Abstract Research is finding that exposure to early math during the baby and toddler stages is valuable for their later mathematical outcomes; however, what this looks like in practice has had relatively limited exploration. In response, this study provides insight into the presence of early math precursors (foundational pre-mathematical skills such as attribute, comparison, change, patterns), as detailed by Hynes-Berry, Chen, & Abel, in six public library storytimes for babies and toddlers. This qualitative descriptive study consisted of naturalistic observations and deductive and inductive coding of video-recorded storytimes. Participants included six library educators, 63 babies and toddlers, and 61 caregivers. The observations revealed that all four early math precursors are present in the storytimes through a variety of methods, strategies, and resources the educators and caregivers used with the babies and toddlers. title: Examining Influence on Early Care and Education Teachers’ Intention to Leave: Compensation, Workplace Support, and Depressive Symptoms
text_snippet: Examining Influence on Early Care and Education Teachers’ Intention to Leave: Compensation, Workplace Support, and Depressive Symptoms Abstract High turnover among early care and education (ECE) teachers threatens workforce stability and may have negative implications for ECE program quality and children’s early learning and development. Previous research limited to specific regions or small samples has linked low compensation, workplace support, and mental well-being to teacher’ turnover intentions. However, these associations have not yet been examined within nationally representative data. This preregistered study examined the extent to which compensation, workplace support, and depressive symptoms were associated with turnover intention among a nationally representative sample of center-based ECE teachers. It also explore whether depressive symptoms moderated the links between compensation and workplace support and turnover intention. The study relied on data from the 2019 National Survey of Early Care and Education (NSECE) Workforce Questionnaire ( N = 3,379). title: Sustaining Scientific Literacy Among Children Through Play In The Early Years: A Cultural-Historical View
text_snippet: Sustaining Scientific Literacy Among Children Through Play In The Early Years: A Cultural-Historical View Abstract Children gradually develop their scientific literacy through play-based experiences in their early years. Several studies have emphasised the importance of developing children’s scientific literacy in the early years, highlighting the long-term benefits; however, sustaining scientific literacy to achieve greater benefits in subsequent stages remains an area that has yet to be adequately addressed in the research literature. This study explores how educators can support children in moving from developing to sustaining scientific literacy through play-based experiences in the early years. Using digital visual observation as part of a qualitative research design to understand the process and relationships, video data were collected and analysed from three similar play activities at a regional early childhood centre in Australia, followed by short, informal interviews with educators. title: Teaching Science Through Play: An Adaptive Professional Development Programme to Provide Tailored Support to Preschool Teachers
text_snippet: Teaching Science Through Play: An Adaptive Professional Development Programme to Provide Tailored Support to Preschool Teachers Abstract Even though play is commonplace in preschool education, a need is constantly highlighted to support preschool teachers in integrating concrete play-based methods and models for science teaching. However, this support needs to be tailored to the special professional needs, challenges, and educational contexts of preschool teachers. Drawing upon Fleer’s Conceptual PlayWorlds (CPW) model, this study examines preschool teachers’ collective design of CPW science activities within the context of a Professional Development (PD) program involving 28 in-service preschool teachers from six kindergartens in Greece, which are examined as six different cases. Teachers’ idiosyncratic needs and preferences along with researchers’ in situ support, have been explored through qualitative content analysis of whole-group/small-group discussions and post-reflections. Findings revealed that teachers exhibited a range of needs and styles when designing science activities within the CPW’s settings. The ways the researchers reflected on the diverse needs and styles to provide adaptive support based on teachers’ idiosyncratic characteristics were highlighted. title: Hidden Boundaries: A Case Study of Perspectives On Family-School Partnerships in a Multicultural Classroom
text_snippet: Hidden Boundaries: A Case Study of Perspectives On Family-School Partnerships in a Multicultural Classroom Abstract This qualitative case study explores the hidden boundaries within family school partnerships in a multicultural early childhood classroom by examining the perspectives of two teachers and two parents from diverse cultural backgrounds. Conducted at a public preschool serving predominantly immigrant families, the study employed semi-structured interviews to investigate how cultural backgrounds shape understandings of family engagement. Findings reveal significant misalignments between participants' conceptualizations: while the White head teacher emphasized visible, school-based participation, immigrant parents and the Congolese teaching assistant valued trust-based relationships and home-based support that often remained invisible within traditional frameworks. While the study highlights the vital role of culturally aligned staff as intermediaries, it also reveals that such mediated communication often remains transactional rather than transformative. title: Screening Preschoolers’ Play and Participation in Early Childhood Education and Care Services: A Feasibility Study
text_snippet: Screening Preschoolers’ Play and Participation in Early Childhood Education and Care Services: A Feasibility Study Abstract Play and participation are key for children’s wellbeing and development. Children who may be at risk of developmental delays can exhibit limited play skills and have difficulty participating in play whist attending early education and care centres (ECECs). A Play and Participation Screening Service (PPSS) was developed and piloted in ECECs to detect children requiring additional supports. A mixed methods feasibility study using action research evaluated the feasibility of the screening tool using five criteria (acceptability, practicality, implementation, preliminary efficacy and demand) and explored barriers families encounter accessing supports. The PPSS was implemented sequentially across four ECECs with learnings taken from each setting and applied into subsequent settings. A total of 14 families completed the screening and feedback session and 13 completed screening interview, feedback session and ongoing support sessions. Caregivers and educators reported the service was acceptable and practical. Other feasibility criteria were partially met (implementation and preliminary efficacy), and one was not met (demand). title: Early Childhood Educators’ Understanding of Intrafamilial Violence and the Impact of Exposure on the Developing Child
text_snippet: Early Childhood Educators’ Understanding of Intrafamilial Violence and the Impact of Exposure on the Developing Child Abstract Disturbing statistics indicate an increasing prevalence of intrafamilial violence in Australia with one in three Australian women being victim-survivors of intrafamilial violence (Australian Bureau of Statistics [ABS], 2023). Many of these victim-survivors have children who are also directly or indirectly impacted. Increases in all forms of intrafamilial violence mean that victim-survivors, particularly children, experience unprecedented physical, psychological, emotional, and social consequences of exposure. In light of the high rate of intrafamilial violence in Australia, and the government’s commitment to accessible child-care and early years learning, it is highly possible that early childhood teachers and other educators will interact with children who experience intrafamilial violence. As children who live with intrafamilial violence bring the trauma they experience to their early childhood education and care service, early childhood educators must have the skills and confidence to recognise the signs of exposure to intrafamilial violence and be ready to support children and foster their educational journey. title: Recommended Practices in Early Intervention: a Mixed Methods Exploration of Provider Perspectives on Family-Centered and Capacity-Building Practices
text_snippet: Recommended Practices in Early Intervention: a Mixed Methods Exploration of Provider Perspectives on Family-Centered and Capacity-Building Practices Abstract Early intervention providers work with children 0–3 and their families and come from a variety of disciplines. To better understand how providers enact family-centered and capacity-building practices in their work, we surveyed 95 providers in Illinois and conducted 19 follow-up interviews. Within the survey, participants responded to 15 Likert-type items. We analyzed the qualitative survey and interview data to determine themes, showing that (1) EI providers have expectations that families be both passive and active participants in services; (2) EI providers hold both strengths-based and judgment-based views of families; (3) EI providers value routines-based and specialized materials when providing services to children and families; (4) EI providers value connecting families to resources but may view some resources as outside their role; (5) EI providers collaborate with families by getting their input and building their capacities; and (6) EI providers’ professional and personal qualities set the stage for family-centered and capacity-building practices. title: Learning to Notice Quality Interactions: Preservice Teachers’ Sense-Making of Multilingual Family Engagement in Community-Based Fieldwork
text_snippet: Learning to Notice Quality Interactions: Preservice Teachers’ Sense-Making of Multilingual Family Engagement in Community-Based Fieldwork Abstract This study examines what became salient in preservice teachers’ (PSTs’) written sense-making as they conducted community-based observations of multilingual families in a children’s museum, and how they interpreted families’ language and literacy practices through written fieldwork artifacts. Situated within the Family Learning Observation and Analysis (FLOA) project, we analyzed 39 artifacts (fieldnotes, video analyses, and analytic reports) produced by 13 English-monolingual early childhood PSTs during a Spring 2025 museum-based field experience. Using multiple cycles of qualitative coding, we examined the interactional features that PSTs repeatedly treated as consequential for children’s engagement and participation. Three interconnected themes emerged across PSTs’ written sense-making: relational presence, translanguaging, and multimodal meaning-making. title: The Frequency of Teachers’ Linguistic Strategies Across Classroom Contexts and Teachers in Preschool Settings During the Summer
text_snippet: The Frequency of Teachers’ Linguistic Strategies Across Classroom Contexts and Teachers in Preschool Settings During the Summer Abstract Guided by Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, which posits that children learn through their interactions with others, this study examined how frequently teachers used linguistic strategies designed to promote rich teacher-child conversations in preschool classrooms during the summer months. The participants were six teachers from three preschool centers in a Northeastern state of the United States. These centers served children (ages 3-5) from low- and middle-income backgrounds. Teacher-child conversations were video-recorded in each of the three classroom contexts: mealtimes, free play, and group time, on three different days. An interval-based coding system was adopted to code the frequency of eight linguistic strategies. Findings indicated that teachers used most of the linguistic strategies infrequently, particularly those designed to foster rich teacher-child conversations, such as asking wh-questions and using language modeling strategies (e.g., “expand” and “extend”). title: Shifting the Paradigm: From ‘Best Practice’ to ‘Best Beliefs’ for Autism Within Inclusive Early Childhood Education
text_snippet: Shifting the Paradigm: From ‘Best Practice’ to ‘Best Beliefs’ for Autism Within Inclusive Early Childhood Education Abstract This study explores the role of early childhood teachers’ beliefs in shaping inclusive practices for autistic children within Australian early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings. While national frameworks such as the Early Years Learning Framework (AGDE, 2022) and the National Guidelines: Best Practice in Early Childhood Intervention (Reimagine Australia, 2024) emphasise specific practices or ‘best practice’ as the foundation for inclusion, the lived experiences of many autistic children suggest a persistent and concerning gap between policy and practice. Drawing on a qualitative case study of five degree-qualified early childhood teachers identified for their strong commitment to inclusion, this research investigated the underlying beliefs guiding their pedagogies. Semi-structured interviews revealed several interrelated themes concerning inclusive pedagogy in ECEC. The findings suggest that authentic inclusion may be more effectively facilitated through a shift in discourse, from “best practice” to “best beliefs”, where educators’ core philosophies, rather than prescriptive techniques, drive inclusive pedagogy. title: Parental Support of Preschool Children’s Early Writing Using a Researcher-designed Writing Notebook as a Tool
text_snippet: Parental Support of Preschool Children’s Early Writing Using a Researcher-designed Writing Notebook as a Tool Abstract Research suggests that preschool children who come into kindergarten with foundational skills in reading and writing have a literacy advantage. Unfortunately, there are few opportunities in the preschool classroom where early writing occurs. Therefore, this study employed a design-based research method to aid parents in supporting their preschoolers’ early writing while using a researcher-designed Writing Notebook. The sample, which was selected using a convenience sampling technique, included six parents and their six children from the 3K classroom and five parents and their six children from the 4K classroom in a local child development center in the Southeastern region of the United States. The 3K classroom serves three-year-old children, while the 4K classroom serves four-year-old children. Specifically, this paper addressed two questions: (1) How did parents scaffold instruction to move children from their present stage to increasingly meaningful writing exploration? and (2) What was the association between children’s writing and parental support? title: “But how does flying work on gravity when you just go up?”: An Investigation of Children’s Science Questions While Reading Life and Physical Science Books in Early Childhood
text_snippet: “But how does flying work on gravity when you just go up?”: An Investigation of Children’s Science Questions While Reading Life and Physical Science Books in Early Childhood Abstract Children’s question-asking during early childhood plays a central role in cognitive development, reflecting children’s natural curiosity about the world. While research on early science learning has focused on informal contexts (e.g., home) where adults play a key role, less is known about children’s own contributions during these interactions, particularly across different science domains. Our study investigated how children aged 4 to 7 years engage in scientific inquiry by comparing the types of questions children asked while reading a life science book and a physical science book. We recorded 93 mother–child dyads reading two science books from the popular Let’s-Read-and-Find-Out-Science series. Transcribed utterances were coded for five types of science questions. Repeated-measures ANOVAs revealed that children asked more science-related questions during the physical science book than the life science book, with explanation- and fact-seeking questions being the most prevalent within both books. title: Writing Identity and Self-Efficacy in Early Childhood Across Home and School Contexts
text_snippet: Writing Identity and Self-Efficacy in Early Childhood Across Home and School Contexts Abstract Early writing development involves more than acquiring transcriptional skills; it is closely bound up with the emergence of children's identities as writers and their beliefs in their own capacity to write. Drawing on sociocultural theory and social cognitive theory, this study examined how young children construct writing self-efficacy and writer identity in relation to how parents and educators define and recognize early writing. A convergent mixed-methods design was used to triangulate data from 245 four-year-old children, 87 educators, and 156 parents in public preschool settings in Greece. Semi-structured interviews with children, supported by visual prompts depicting five developmental writing stages (drawing, scribbling, letter strings, invented spelling, and conventional spelling), were paired with parallel educator and parent surveys assessing recognition of, and rationales for, writing at each stage. title: A Pedagogy of Presence: Material Encounters with Infants and Toddlers
text_snippet: A Pedagogy of Presence: Material Encounters with Infants and Toddlers Abstract This article introduces a Pedagogy of Presence framework developed through a qualitative case study exploring visual arts pedagogy with infants and toddlers in four early childhood education (ECE) settings in Aotearoa New Zealand. The study examined how teachers design and facilitate meaningful material encounters with infants and toddlers, emphasising relational pedagogy, material exploration, and teachers’ image of the child. Drawing on interviews, observations, and pedagogical documentation, we found that teachers engaged in a responsive ‘dance’ of listening, echoing, and provoking new ideas and thinking, underpinned by a foundation of attuned care. Organisational structures and thoughtfully designed environments enabled sustained engagement, while teachers’ inquiries and collaborative dialogue supported ongoing pedagogical growth. title: Arts Education and Cognitive and Socio-emotional Development in Early Childhood Education: A Scoping Review
text_snippet: Arts Education and Cognitive and Socio-emotional Development in Early Childhood Education: A Scoping Review Abstract Arts education (AE) in early childhood school settings has been increasingly recognized as a pedagogical environment that supports a range of cognitive and socio-emotional processes, including creativity, critical thinking, self-regulation, and a sense of belonging. This study aims to map and synthesize recent empirical literature (2018–2024) on arts education practices integrated into early childhood education, including visual arts, music, dance, and theater. A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with searches performed in Scopus and Web of Science (WoS). The analysis focused on identifying types of interventions, methodological approaches, and reported cognitive and socio-emotional outcomes across studies. The findings reveal recurring patterns in the literature linking participation in AE with a variety of developmental processes, particularly in the domains of well-being, educational innovation, and socio-emotional development. title: Family Matters: Expanding the Dimensions of Quality in Early Childhood and Care
text_snippet: Family Matters: Expanding the Dimensions of Quality in Early Childhood and Care Abstract Family involvement is a key component of educational quality, particularly in Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC). It strengthens home–school relationships, supports children’s well-being and learning, and lays the foundation for subsequent academic success. However, most quality assessment frameworks mainly focus on structural or process-related setting characteristics, while giving limited consideration to family involvement. This study addresses this gap through the development and implementation of a complementary instrument —the Family Involvement in Early Childhood Education Module (FIECE-M)— designed to be used alongside the ITERS-3 and ECERS-3 scales. A quantitative and cross-sectional design was employed, with data collected from 28 ECEC rooms, from 13 centres in Spain, involving 42 educators and 302 children. Results reveal overall good quality and moderate-to-high family involvement levels. Significant differences emerged according to centre size, educational cycle, and room type. title: A Three-Level Socioecological Framework for Culturally Anchored SEL Practices: Self-Reflection, Collaborative Learning, and Professional Partnerships
text_snippet: A Three-Level Socioecological Framework for Culturally Anchored SEL Practices: Self-Reflection, Collaborative Learning, and Professional Partnerships Abstract Social and emotional learning (SEL) is increasingly recognized as a foundational component of whole-child development, supporting not only individual well-being but also broader social and emotional well-being. Social and emotional competencies, as fostered through SEL, are widely recognized as critical in early childhood. This is particularly the case during the preschool years (ages 3–5), a period characterized by rapid growth across key developmental domains. Thus, integrating SEL into teaching practice in early childhood education (ECE) is crucial for supporting young children’s holistic development. Furthermore, as classrooms in the United States become increasingly diverse, there is an urgent need for early childhood teachers to design and implement culturally responsive SEL experiences for young children. In this conceptual article, informed by Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory, I propose a three-level socioecological framework for teacher development of culturally anchored SEL practices, comprising self-reflection at the individual level, collaborative learning at the group level, and professional partnerships at the community level. title: Association Between Intergenerational Care Facility Attendance and Developmental Outcomes in Preschoolers
text_snippet: Association Between Intergenerational Care Facility Attendance and Developmental Outcomes in Preschoolers Abstract Interaction with older adults is considered important for children’s development, yet empirical evidence on preschoolers’ interactions in intergenerational environments remains limited. This exploratory pilot study aimed to compare the developmental outcomes among children attending integrated intergenerational care facilities and those in stand-alone facilities. Data were obtained from the parents/guardians of 205 preschoolers aged 4–6 years. Child development was assessed using the Kinder Infant Development Scale and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. To isolate the unique contribution of the institutional environment, inverse probability of treatment weighting was employed to statistically adjust for multiple covariates, including children’s demographic characteristics, parental socioeconomic status, and domestic intergenerational factors. The results indicated that attendance at intergenerational care facilities, characterized by routine and structured exposure to older adults, was significantly associated with improved fine motor development. title: ‘I’ll Just Watch You For Now’: Exploring the Role of Place in Supporting Young Children’s Creativity in Online STEM Learning Environments
text_snippet: ‘I’ll Just Watch You For Now’: Exploring the Role of Place in Supporting Young Children’s Creativity in Online STEM Learning Environments Abstract The learning environment has a meaningful impact on young children’s creativity. However, while research has explored the physical environment in terms of fostering creativity, less is known about online learning contexts. This article reports on the elements of the online learning environment that fostered young children’s creativity, specifically during STEM activities. In this case study, a group of first grade children in regional Australia engaged in a range of activities delivered online synchronously by a Science Discovery Centre (SDC) 700 km away. Guided by the A-E of Children’s Creativity framework, both multimodal video analysis and semi-structured interviews with all participants explored the learning environment element of place that supported the young children’s creative thinking. Based upon the findings, a series of recommendations are presented, designed to assist educators and service providers in preparing the learning environment to support young children’s creative STEM thinking in the online setting.

title: A Critical Realist Explanation of Chinese Early Childhood Teachers’ Professional Identity
text_snippet: A Critical Realist Explanation of Chinese Early Childhood Teachers’ Professional Identity Abstract Early childhood teachers’ professional identity is critical to defining how teachers work on advancing young children’s learning in society. However, the literature suggests that research on this topic is insufficient in non-Western countries such as China and overlooks the mechanisms underlying teachers’ professional identity. This study is informed by critical realism and includes qualitative interviews and policy document analysis to examine Chinese early childhood teachers’ professional identity perceived by teachers and policymakers. It also employs critical realism to construct theoretical explanations of social interactions and the generative mechanisms underlying those perceptions. Caring, pedagogical, partnership and leadership, and learning roles are identified. Five social interactions and mechanisms are proposed to explain teachers’ professional identity. Implications for research, policy, and practice are discussed.

title: Providing Universal and Continuous Support for Identified and Unidentified Vulnerable Children in Preschool Settings
text_snippet: Providing Universal and Continuous Support for Identified and Unidentified Vulnerable Children in Preschool Settings Abstract Early childhood education offers meaningful settings for promoting resilience and positive development, especially among children facing early life adversities. Vulnerable situations put children at risk for physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development. Early childhood educators are primary sources of support for vulnerable children, as much of children’s awake hours are spent at preschools. However, some families may not disclose their vulnerable situations or some of their situations may not make them eligible for formal support. Nonetheless, early childhood education can use approaches that provide universal support to children regardless of whether they are or are not in vulnerable situations and whether those situations are known and identified or unknown and unidentified. We provide four main areas of universal support that are undemanding and simple to implement into daily classroom routines that will benefit children with identified and unidentified vulnerabilities.

title: Discovering Strategies to Support Families and Educators in Joining Together to Implement Interventions for Disruptive Behavior in Preschool: Innovation Tournaments
text_snippet: Discovering Strategies to Support Families and Educators in Joining Together to Implement Interventions for Disruptive Behavior in Preschool: Innovation Tournaments Abstract The preschool years represent a critical early intervention period for disruptive behaviors characteristic of externalizing disorders. Despite the promise of intervening early, interventions for disruptive behavior are challenging for families and preschool teachers to implement. In partnership with preschools, our team is using the discover, design/build, and test (DDBT) framework to develop a new intervention, the Parent-Educator Action Response (PEAR), to support teachers and families in joining together to implement interventions for disruptive behavior across home and preschool. This paper presents results from the discover stage. Innovation tournaments (ITs) were conducted in two metropolitan cities with legal guardians of a preschool-age child ( n = 77) and preschool teachers ( n = 33) to identify barriers to and strategies for joining together to implement behavioral interventions for disruptive behavior. Go-Zone plots were utilized to identify strategies with the highest feasibility and importance. title: Teaching Toward Equity: Kindergarten Teachers’ Responses to Readiness Variation and Preschool Skill Gaps
text_snippet: Teaching Toward Equity: Kindergarten Teachers’ Responses to Readiness Variation and Preschool Skill Gaps Abstract This study explores how kindergarten teachers interpret and respond to the wide range of school readiness skills present in their classrooms. Building on a national survey of 422 kindergarten teachers, we conducted in-depth interviews with 26 teachers across 22 states to understand how they make instructional decisions when faced with heterogeneous skill profiles. Findings reveal that teachers engage in fairness-driven instructional triage, focusing primarily on students with the greatest needs. While preschool experience was seen as beneficial, its perceived impact was conditional on program type and home environment. The study highlights how teachers’ instructional priorities contribute to skill convergence over the kindergarten year and suggests system-level supports are needed to promote growth for all students.

title: Refugee Families’ Resources for Children’s Education: A Dynamic Use of the Community Cultural Wealth Model
text_snippet: Refugee Families’ Resources for Children’s Education: A Dynamic Use of the Community Cultural Wealth Model Abstract The accelerating trend of large-scale displacement and forced migration of people around the world has created an urgent need for access to quality education for children with refugee status in resettlement contexts, as well as a need for innovative and responsive ways to support their families. In this article, using two years of data collected from research on the border between Türkiye and Syria, we explored the knowledge and understanding of 54 refugee families from Syria, Iraq, Iran, and Ukraine in supporting their children’s education in Türkiye, which has been one of the largest resettlement countries. We employed qualitative methods and collected data from families through semi-structured interviews, facilitated by educational journey maps and picture books, in the context of multilingual family mathematics workshops. In these workshops, families, teachers, and children came together to engage in mathematics activities and conversations about forced migration and broader life experiences in relation to their children’s education. title: Coaching Caregivers to Implement Naturalistic Strategies to Teach Imitation Skills
text_snippet: Coaching Caregivers to Implement Naturalistic Strategies to Teach Imitation Skills Abstract Imitation, the ability to copy someone else’s actions or words, is a pivotal skill developed in early childhood. Developing imitation skills has cascading benefits for developing social skills, communication skills, and play skills. Autistic children may have difficulties in developing imitation skills which can lead to delays in communication and play skills development. Naturalistic developmental behavioral interventions (NDBI) are interventions that leverage a child’s interests and use play to teach various skills to children with developmental disabilities, including autism. A variety of NDBI strategies leverage imitation and teach imitation skills. Coaching and behavior skills training (BST) are evidence-based practices for teaching caregivers to implement interventions, including NDBI. Following the fictional story of early childhood special educator, Mikhail, a young autistic boy, Gabriel, and Gabriel’s parents, Tanya and George, this article explores how early childhood educators can leverage coaching practices with caregivers to implement NDBI to promote imitation skills development.

title: Dialogic Shared Reading with Visual Phonics to Support Language and Emergent Literacy in Diverse Learners: Theoretical Foundation and Practice-Based Guidance
text_snippet: Dialogic Shared Reading with Visual Phonics to Support Language and Emergent Literacy in Diverse Learners: Theoretical Foundation and Practice-Based Guidance Abstract This practitioner article presents a home-based instructional approach that combines Dialogic Shared Reading (DSR) and Visual Phonics (VP) to support emergent literacy and language development for culturally, linguistically, and neurologically diverse young children. The approach strengthens parents as active agents in their child’s early literacy and language learning by focusing on a child with attention challenges who is acquiring more than one language. This article outlines a practical, family-led model derived from implementing these strategies with a bilingual preschooler. It demonstrates a structured framework for integrating DSR, an interactive reading method that encourages verbal engagement, with VP, a multisensory system utilizing visual-kinesthetic cues for phonemes. We explain in detail how we: (1) implement DSR in bilingual homes to promote language and literacy transfer; (2) introduce VP to increase phonological awareness; and (3) establish a daily reading routine. Ultimately, this guide underlines the parent’s role as a practitioner and illustrates how structured parent-child interactions can foster a child’s overall development.

title: Do We Align? Parents’ and Teachers’ Perceptions of Dual Language Learners’ Social Competence in Preschool
text_snippet: Do We Align? Parents’ and Teachers’ Perceptions of Dual Language Learners’ Social Competence in Preschool Abstract Understanding dual language learners’ (DLLs’) social competence across home and school settings is essential to provide tailored support. This qualitative study, using data collected from three early care programs, examined parents’ and teachers’ perceptions of DLLs’ social competence and explored the challenges and resources needed to foster this social competence. Participants observed that DLLs often behave differently across home and school settings, which is likely shaped by sociocultural and linguistic factors. Findings also revealed both shared and divergent perspectives among parents and teachers regarding DLLs’ social competence, likely influenced by their cultural backgrounds and life experiences. The findings of this study underscore the complexity of DLLs’ social functioning in culturally and linguistically diverse environments. Notably, although monolingual children were not the focus of this study, some teacher participants raised broader concerns about how all children navigate culturally and linguistically diverse environments, highlighting the importance of supporting both DLLs and monolingual children’s interactions in multilingual settings. title: Text Messaging Programs to Support Family Literacy Practices: A Scoping Review
text_snippet: Text Messaging Programs to Support Family Literacy Practices: A Scoping Review Abstract Using bulk digital text messaging has been shown to be effective in many different fields such as health program interventions and supporting parents/carers. Evaluations of these interventions indicate positive changes in practice; however, it appears the potential of digital messaging through short message services (SMS) have not been fully taken advantage of in early childhood education. This scoping review using Arksey and O’Malley’s (2005) approach investigates the current practices of text messaging programs to support families in the development of preschool aged children’s language and literacy learning. Searches of five databases identified 16 articles that fitted our criteria. Results indicate: (1) digital text messaging programs are an under-utilised tool for supporting families in preschool education, (2) there is a scarcity of peer-reviewed research exploring the use of text messaging programs in early childhood education, (3) text messaging programs are helpful in increasing parent-child interactions and supporting home literacy practices and, (4) engaging parents and/or caregivers via text messaging programs can be a highly effective home-school transition st

title: Unlocking Imaginative Play: A Scoping Review Investigating Early Childhood Educators’ Contributions Towards Imaginative Play
text_snippet: Unlocking Imaginative Play: A Scoping Review Investigating Early Childhood Educators’ Contributions Towards Imaginative Play Abstract Play is a core occupation in childhood, essential for promoting cognitive, social, and emotional development. Imaginative play is essential for enriching a child’s communication, problem-solving, and emotional regulation. Despite the benefits imaginative play has for children, there remains a need to explore the facilitators and barriers that exist for early childhood educators to support imaginative play activities. This scoping review synthesized existing literature on the enabling and inhibiting factors related to educators and their involvement in imaginative play with young children. Scopus, PubMed, ERIC, and APA PsycNET databases were selected and searched. A total of 14 articles published between 2008 and 2021 were retrieved for data extraction. Meta-ethnography analysis was used to establish the facilitators and barriers that contribute towards imaginative play. Facilitators included fostering environments, adult participation, and scaffolding imaginative play experiences. title: Interactions for Equity: Parents’ Perspectives on Online Heritage Language Learning
text_snippet: Interactions for Equity: Parents’ Perspectives on Online Heritage Language Learning Abstract Quality family–educator partnerships are central to equitable outcomes in Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC). For culturally and linguistically diverse communities, sustaining children’s heritage language is an important dimension of early learning and identity. While online platforms are increasingly used to connect families and educators, little is known about how parents experience their role in such initiatives. This qualitative study investigated Farsi-speaking parents’ perspectives on a Zoom-mediated heritage language program in Australia. Seven parents participated in six online sessions with their children, followed by semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed thematically. Findings show that parents navigated proximity and autonomy in supporting their children, provided scaffolding and clarification during literacy tasks, and used songs, routines, and rewards to sustain motivation. Parents also described how everyday practices reinforced cultural identity and how the facilitator’s authority, responsiveness, and encouragement shaped engagement. title: Oral Storytelling and Emergent Critical Thinking in Early Childhood
text_snippet: Oral Storytelling and Emergent Critical Thinking in Early Childhood Abstract In a time characterised by widespread misinformation and the increasing sophistication of artificial intelligence, the capacity to think critically has become a foundational educational priority. While critical thinking initiatives have largely focused on adolescents and adults, far less attention has been paid to how such dispositions can be nurtured in early childhood. This paper draws on design-based doctoral research conducted in two preschool classrooms to explore how oral storytelling can serve as a dialogic and responsive pedagogical practice for fostering emergent critical thinking in young children. The present study offers a distinct focus on the pedagogical conditions through which critical thinking is enacted. Across a 10-week intervention, educators implemented structured oral storytelling sessions emphasising open-ended questioning, perspective-taking, and collaborative problem-solving. Data were generated through classroom observation, video recordings, audio-recorded transcripts, and collaborative researcher/educator reflection. title: Training Early Childhood Educators to Observe, Assess and Enhance Discrete Play Skills
text_snippet: Training Early Childhood Educators to Observe, Assess and Enhance Discrete Play Skills Abstract This intervention study describes how 39 early childhood teachers from Pennsylvania learned to observe, assess, and enhance discrete sensorimotor, functional, and symbolic play skills by completing the DiscoveryScape Play Training (DSPT), a professional development course grounded in developmental play theory. While several instruments and training programs address play broadly, the present study presents an integrated model: a short teacher-training course targeting discrete play-skill development, together with a dedicated observational instrument to measure children’s play-skill progression called the Qualitative Characteristics of Children’s Play (QCCP). A retrospective pre-test design was utilized to determine the effectiveness of DiscoveryScape Play Training (DSPT). Findings suggest that the training was associated with significant and meaningful increases in teachers’ self-reported beliefs, knowledge and skills related to observing, assessing, and enhancing children’s play skill development (0.77 average effect size). Follow-up survey analysis revealed significant additional gains following 16 weeks of teacher practice observing and assessing children’s play skills.

title: Yoga Storytelling as an Active Learning Approach: Insights from Early Childhood Classroom Practice
text_snippet: Yoga Storytelling as an Active Learning Approach: Insights from Early Childhood Classroom Practice Abstract Movement plays a central role in early childhood learning, supporting children’s physical development, emotional regulation and cognitive engagement. In recent years, educators have been paying more attention to movement-based approaches to enhance classroom learning experiences. Yoga, when adapted for young children, offers opportunities for playful movement, body awareness and relaxation. This paper reflects on my experiences as a movement educator and explores how yoga can support active learning in early childhood classrooms. Drawing on a series of 30-minute yoga storytelling sessions delivered to five- and six-year-old children in a preschool setting, the paper illustrates how yoga storytelling can be integrated into everyday classroom practice to promote active engagement, body awareness, imagination, and self-regulation.
